summary: Establish what Functionary currently is (ops record + implementation), then audit every marketing-site claim against it

truth.summary: Functionary (renamed from Arachne on 2026-09-12) is a local-first tool in which a coding agent writes a "flow" - a program in a restricted, statically checked subset of Rust that can only wire together trusted, pre-built blocks and built-in control structures (Jigs) - and a conventional runtime, not the agent, executes it. The repo README still leads with "a visual canvas for building, running, and auditing information-processing pipelines"; the ops record since 2026-11-15 has moved the centre of gravity to "agents write understandable programs that do your work" with a terminal client (`fnary`) and auto mode as the familiar way in, and the canvas as the surface that makes the program visible and reviewable. The stated problem is that agent work on multi-step knowledge tasks is a transcript, not a declared process: a principal cannot see what was done, skipped steps and unvetted sources contaminate results silently, and nothing can be fixed durably. The answer is bounding (agents compose, they do not implement; inner agents get narrow jobs), a one-to-one canvas/source/execution mapping, provenance and origin on every value, recorded effects (receipts), revision pins and review keys. Users are two archetypes on one line (2026-10-29): the Associate who iterates attended runs, and the Automator who stabilizes flows for unattended runs; formalization and every protection are opt-in. The backend (`functionary-flow-*` crates), the React Flow canvas, `fnary` with auto mode, the run transcript stream, project directories and tenant-policy locality are in code on `bleeding`. Not shipped: there is no release, no license file and no installer; the cross-platform release epic F112 is mid-flight (interpreter crate exists but is not wired into the server; runs today still need rustc and bwrap on Linux). In the last three weeks the positions that moved are: terminal/auto mode became co-equal with or ahead of the canvas, the authoring agent gained the right to run flows, protections flipped from default refusals to opt-in options, the shipped build was ruled interpreter-only, and the flow language surface (Result, match, Judge presets) was re-ruled on 2026-11-16 and is largely unbuilt. The exact phrase "reproducibility is for trust" does not appear in ops; the nearest record is the 2026-10-19 author's account ("easy to replicate as exactly as possible", "costly replications") and the 2026-11-15 premise about control flow living in an auditable program.

claims.claim: What the record says a user exposed to contamination risk needs: durable artifacts, strong audit trails, clear process with permissions at each step, 'easy to replicate as exactly as possible', and easy to adjust after a contamination error. claims.claim: Trust thesis: you do not trust the agent, you bound it (narrow job, limited information); trust is read off the composition; verify the process rather than every run; the process learns, the model does not. claims.claim: Every effect (model call, write, notify) passes one runtime boundary that checks authority, looks up a recorded result, and records a receipt. After a crash a block re-runs and receives its recorded results instead of repeating calls; an external action whose completion was not recorded is reported as Uncertain rather than silently retried.
claims.note: In code 'replay' means crash recovery from recorded results. It is not a claim that re-running a flow gives identical model output. Automatic resume after a crash is not built: 'After a crash, running runs wait for a person to recover them' (Deployment Architecture doc, item 1).

claims.claim: A run is pinned to the exact flow revision, settings and module versions it started with (run definition and run pins), and a human review approval is bound to a review key that changes when source, config, a bound table revision or a block version changes.

claims.claim: Provenance: every value records where it came from (which block run, which inputs, which configuration). A second typing axis, origin, marks each wire as Sourced, Computed, Generated (a model touched it), Verified or Reviewed, so the canvas shows whether a model wrote a value.

vocabulary_current: Functionary: the product (renamed from Arachne 2026-09-12)
fnary: the terminal client for the project agent; `fnary auto` opens auto mode
Flow: one automation, written as one Rust source file in a restricted subset; blocks wired together plus Jigs
Flow source: the restricted-Rust file an agent writes; the single source of truth
Block: a trusted, versioned unit of work implemented by Functionary; one canvas node, one call in source
Block call / its output: current wording for what was 'step' and 'value'
Jig: a visible control structure around a body (Map, Repeat, Retry, Refine; Replicate ruled, not built)
Module: a flow used as a function with typed arguments and return type
Canvas: the visual editor/view of flow source; maps one-to-one to the code that runs
Checker (allowlist checker, screen): static, fail-closed reader of flow source that produces the graph
Graph / IR: the derived representation the runtime executes
Lowering: turning the checked graph into an executable program
Test and Run: Test is a dry run withholding durable writes; Run is real; Escalate promotes a Test to a Run
Auto mode: the authoring agent alternates between editing and running a flow toward a goal
Outer (authoring) agent / project agent: writes flows

truth.summary: Flow source on `bleeding` (7f74919d, 2026-11-17) is a screened Rust-like subset, not yet real Rust: the 2026-11-15 drift investigation compiled 110 reference flows with rustc and 45 failed. "Flow source is real Rust; every accepted flow compiles under rustc against a host-generated prelude" is the ruled standing rule (v3, 2026-11-16), and the work that makes it true (F110: typed rows, `row.field` reads, capitalized settings constants, struct inputs, a rustc agreement gate) sits on `integrate/f110`, 249 commits ahead of `bleeding` and unmerged. A further retyping of every flow is ruled but unbuilt (F114: `Result<T>` fields, `?`, restricted `match` replacing Branch, `a.or(b)` replacing Coalesce, Judge as Model presets, Rust primitives replacing `Number`/`Bool`). The block ontology is structurally stable and in code: seven kinds (Source, Block, Agent, Transform, Jig, Gate, Egress) in one contract crate, with 29 block declarations, 12 transform names, 6 Jigs and 4 procedures; the palette groups mode variants into cards. Origin (Sourced, Computed, Generated, Verified, Reviewed) is computed by the checker for every wire from declarations alone, serialized on every canvas edge and drawn by the web client; a separate label axis (sensitivity, categories, compartments, locality) has its own check pass. The checker is fail-closed: CST screen, IR derivation, declaration-driven contract check; refusals are symbolic span-attributed codes (never values) surfaced as canvas chips and a JSON `diagnostics` array. Source is canonical and the canvas is a derived projection; canvas edits are semantic ops applied as minimal source diffs under a tested isomorphism contract, but the drawing is not one node per source line (palette cards group separately named blocks, pure Transform chains collapse, struct literals project as nodes). The marketing site's snippet (`Field::new(...).input(row)`, `Source::new`, `row: Row`, lowercase settings) matches no accepted flow on either branch; its "seven kinds" claim is still correct; its verb table has three wrong entries (Apply, a single "Source"/"Judge"/"Check"/"Compare" presented as source-level names is a card-level simplification, Coalesce and Branch are ruled for removal) and omits Script, HandleMissing and the Agent block's real name.

claims.claim: The checker is a three-stage fail-closed pipeline over canonical source: lossless CST, then a screen that refuses disallowed constructs before any graph is derived, then IR derivation (byte-for-byte deterministic, no compiler invoked), then a declaration-driven contract check against the block/transform/Jig tables that rejects implicit conversions.
claims.note: Pipeline shape is a structural commitment. What the screen admits is widening under F110/F114 (e.g. `match`, `?`, `&`, turbofish, `use` imports are being admitted).

claims.claim: The screen refuses, wherever they appear, the keywords `for`, `while`, `loop`, `if`, `else`, `match`, `return`, `impl`, `mod`, `const`, `enum`, `trait`, `pub`, `unsafe`, `async`, `macro` and others, all operators and comparisons, `?`, `&`, `#`, closures, literals outside a two-form allowlist, nested items, shadowing, namespace collisions, recursion, function values and non-builder method calls. There are 23 denial codes (e.g. `shadowed_binding`, `computation_denied`, `literal_denied`, `closure_denied`, `unbound_block`, `caller_capture`).
claims.note: The fail-closed posture is stable; this exact list is not. v3 admits `match`, `?`, `&x`, `.clone()`, `enum`, two attributes, and turbofish. A cross-file `use flows::<slug>::<fn>;` import subset is already admitted (D131).

claims.claim: Refusals are reported as symbolic, span-attributed diagnostics: a stable code, the construct concerned, a source span, and optionally a port name, a source wire reference (`node.port`) and a symbolic detail. A diagnostic never echoes an authored value or a config value. A screened-out source yields a canvas projection with no graph and a list of chips; otherwise chips attach to their node or port. The server returns them as a JSON `diagnostics` array (e.g. `{"error": "the flow did not compile", "diagnostics": [...]}`), and the web client renders the code and construct on the card.
claims.note: On bleeding the reported text is a code plus construct name (e.g. `computation_denied (operator)`), not a prose sentence. 'A diagnostic that says what to write instead' is the ruled standard (v3:25) and is being built on F110 (e.g. lowercase settings refused 'with the corrected spelling', v3:88).

claims.claim: Source is canonical and the graph is always derived from it. Canvas edits are semantic ops addressed by stable identity and applied two ways that must agree: as a minimal CST diff on the source (only the touched bytes change) and as a pure edit of the derived graph, with the contract `check_save(apply_source(src, op)).ir == apply_graph(check_save(src).ir, op)` modulo spans. Edits carry a base revision (SHA-256 of raw source bytes); a mismatch is a surfaced conflict, never a silent apply.
claims.note: This is the accurate form of the 'canvas and code are the same thing' claim: one source of truth with a derived view and a tested edit isomorphism.

claims.claim: The canvas-to-source mapping is deterministic and lossless in the source-to-graph direction but is not one drawn node per source statement. The projection is a pure function of the graph IR, its diagnostics and stable identities, and projects byte-identical JSON for the same IR; it has scopes (root plus one per Jig body), nodes, edges and Jigs. Presentation diverges from source in known ways: a palette card groups separately named blocks as modes, pure Transform chains carry a collapse annotation, and a struct literal projects as a record-construction node with one input port per declared field.
claims.note: Further divergence is ruled: 'Equivalent spellings are the same flow when they derive the same graph. One spelling is not a goal' (v3:76), and the canvas forms for `match` and `a.or(b)` are undesigned (v3:277). Say 'the canvas is derived from the source' rather than 'one-to-one'.

claims.claim: Provenance on wires is called Origin. It is a five-value lattice: Sourced (from a Source or a person), Computed (a pure transform of Sourced inputs), Generated (a model is somewhere in the lineage; sticky through Transforms, Template and Map), Verified (a Generated value checked deterministically against a Sourced one), Reviewed (a person approved it). Verified and Reviewed are the only discharges of Generated.

claims.claim: Origin is computed statically by the checker, before any run, from the declarations alone: each declaration has an origin role derived from its kind and whether it calls a model (Sourced, Generated, Join, Passthrough, Reviewed, VerifiedGate), and a single join table decides how origins combine. The map holds no value, authored string or config. The CheckQuote gate carries the Verified rule; Review produces Reviewed. Format is the one transform that keeps a Sourced input Sourced.

claims.claim: Every canvas edge carries its origin as a required field, and the web client labels edges with it ('Generated: a model is in this value's lineage', 'Verified: a generated value checked against a source', and so on), so whether a model wrote a value is visible before a run.

Origin floors (an Egress refusing a value whose origin is too low, diagnostic `origin_below_floor`) are implemented in the checker with one floor, KnowledgeCommit (requires Verified or Reviewed), but no production declaration carries a floor yet.
claims.note: Do not claim on the site that unverified model output is blocked from being written to knowledge; the mechanism exists, the enforcement is not switched on in the production catalog.

claims.claim: A second, independent axis travels with values: the Label (sensitivity Public/Internal/Confidential/Restricted, data categories, compartments, and locality, the loosest ring a value may reach). A locality check pass reports at check time a refusal that is certain at run time; when the tenant does not enforce locality the run records the crossing instead. Redact and Declassify are the gates that lower a label.

truth.summary: On `bleeding` (HEAD 7f74919d, 2026-11-17) a run is a compiled, pinned artifact executed in a per-run sandboxed runner whose every effect passes one host-side boundary (`Ctx::run`) that journals save-before-act. Each run gets its own directory of SQLite stores (journal.db, outcomes.db, waits.db, status.db) plus a run-index row holding mode, status, compile key, the pinned run definition JSON, the flow source revision, the starter and any fixture hash. The journal holds one entry per block occurrence (request fingerprint + terminal outcome value), an effective-config snapshot per occurrence, and write-once sub-receipts for each model call, tool call and deterministic check. Replay is implemented and is the system's core reproducibility mechanism: a settled entry with the same SHA-256 request fingerprint returns the recorded value and dispatches nothing; a changed request is `OperationMismatch`; an intent with no terminal is `Uncertain` and is never blindly repeated. That means the system does not claim models are deterministic: it records model output once and reuses the record (resume, recover, and Test-to-Run escalation), and treats a fresh model call as new output that needs its own check or review. Test is a dry run of the same pinned artifact with write, notify and knowledge-commit sinks swapped for no-op sinks; a completed Test can be escalated to a Run that reuses the Test's read and compute receipts so only the withheld effects execute. Fixtures, snapshot baselines with per-terminal diff, a fixture suite and branch coverage exist as server routes (regression testing against recorded inputs); there is no general "diff run A against run B" or "re-run this run from scratch on the same inputs" route. Origin tracking (Sourced/Computed/Generated/Verified/Reviewed) is computed statically by the checker and reported on the run record, deterministic Check blocks and output-bound human review exist and work, but the rule that a knowledge commit refuses undischarged Generated values is not wired in production (no block declares the floor yet). The flow-language surface around outcomes (`Outcome<T>` to `Result<T>`, Branch to `match`, Replicate diversity, Judge) was re-ruled on 2026-11-16 and is not built, so outcome vocabulary and several block names are in flux while the journal/receipt/pin/replay substrate is stable.

claims.claim: Every effect in a run goes through one host-side boundary, `Ctx::run`, in a fixed sequence: cancel check, authority check, replay lookup, pause check, admission + budget reservation + second authority check, save an Intent, dispatch to the trusted block, save the terminal outcome before any dependant progresses. Generated flow code never sees the journal, stores, credentials or policies.
claims.note: Decision basis D44/D82 (ops/backend-refactor/decisions.md:979-996).

claims.claim: The run journal is durable (SQLite, one journal.db per run) and holds at most one entry per block occurrence, keyed by `NodePath` (node id plus row / round / call-site segments). Entry kinds: Intent (request about to dispatch), Parked (durable wait, no side effect yet), Settled (request fingerprint + terminal outcome value), Control (host structural decisions such as a branch selection, round, retry), SubReceipt (a sub-step of a block).

Each run has its own directory of stores: journal.db (receipts), outcomes.db (values, paged tables, content-addressed payloads), waits.db (durable timers/reviews) and status.db, plus an append-only crossings file and the locality policy the run started under.

The run index row records, per run: flow id, mode (`test` or `run`), status (running / complete / parked / cancelled / failed), terminal result JSON, error, compile key, compile-cache hit, the pinned run definition as JSON, parent dry run (if escalated), fixture id + content hash, the flow source revision hash, who started it (user, human-or-agent, agent id, session), who resumed it, and whether the host started it unattended.

A request fingerprint is a SHA-256 over a canonical, length-prefixed, variant-tagged encoding of (block name, resolved config, canonical input); blocks that send prompts to a model also fold in the prompt regime (block prompt set and system-prompt delivery). It is the identity the journal checks on replay. It is explicitly a request identity, not a security primitive.

Replay is implemented. On re-driving an occurrence: a Settled entry with the same fingerprint returns the recorded outcome and dispatches nothing; a Parked entry with the same fingerprint is re-driven (it had no side effect); a bare Intent with no terminal settles as `Uncertain` and is not repeated; any saved entry whose fingerprint differs fails as `OperationMismatch` before any new effect.
claims.note: This is replay of recorded results (resume/recover/escalate), not re-execution of the model.

claims.claim: Before each effect the effective configuration is snapshotted per occurrence: every effective field with its value, the settings record and owner that supplied it, the edit revision read, the binding revision followed, parser id and version, and any organisation rule violations (flagged, never silently changed).
claims.note: The stronger requirement that a run records where each value came from across nested module overrides (module default vs call-site override) is ruled 2026-11-16 and not built (F114.16): ops/backend-refactor/architecture.md:99-154.

claims.claim: "Receipt" has a specific meaning: the durable journal record of one non-deterministic effect, used for replay and review. Sub-receipts are write-once records beneath a block occurrence at host-built keys (`<occurrence>/step=i` for a model step, `/step=i/call=j` for a tool call, `/step=i/refused=k` for a refused step, `<occurrence>/receipt=0` for a deterministic block's own receipt). An intent is saved before the sub-step acts and becomes terminal exactly once; a second write is refused; a read with a different request hash is a typed mismatch; keys are never built from model output.

For a `Model` block call the record is: each model call as a sub-receipt holding the round (0 proposal, 1 repair), the model's full reply text, the model name the endpoint reports, the system prompt revision (e.g. `block-model-v1`), the block prompt set and how the system prompt was delivered; plus an occurrence receipt listing, per schema field, whether it holds a value, failed or is absent, whether it came from the repair call, the source anchor of the verified quote, and the typed cause of a failure.
claims.note: Record structure is stable; the Model block's input/output shape is being changed by the 2026-11-16 rulings (Model returns its struct, Judge becomes a Model preset; F114.19, not built).

claims.claim: The Model block does not take the model's word for extracted values: for each field the model must supply a value and a supporting quote, trusted code checks the quote is an exact substring of the input, a failed quote gets one repair call inside the same occurrence, and a field whose quote still fails settles as a failed field of the record. The row is kept and the call does not fail.

An inner `Agent` block's loop is journaled step by step (each model step and each tool call is a sub-receipt, with per-step budget and admission). A crashed or resumed agent occurrence replays its recorded steps instead of regenerating them. A person with View on the flow can read the finished run's agent trace including each step's assistant text, tool calls and tool results; an agent credential is refused that route.

claims.claim: A run pins its definition at start and the pin is immutable. The pinned `RunDefinition` holds: the span-free `ir_hash` (sha256 of the flow's meaning), pinned block/operation versions, table schema refinements, resolved defaults, pinned table revisions, policies in force, pinned effect destinations, module versions and each module call site's parameter mapping, and private-model revision numbers. A fixture-fed run also pins `fixture = <id>@sha256:<hash>`.

claims.claim: A restart, recovery or escalation re-derives the definition and refuses if it differs from the stored pin (`PinError::DefinitionChanged`, naming the first differing field). A changed flow is refused, never recompiled and run under new semantics.

The compiled artifact is content-addressed: the compile key is `sha256:` over the ir_hash, block versions, module pins and call sites, the generated source and the linked libraries, and deliberately excludes spans, comments, dynamic pins and resource caps. Artifacts are cached per tenant directory; the key itself names no tenant.

Stored values are content-addressed: every outcome and table cell carries a `value_hash` (SHA-256 of the one canonical value encoding), payloads live in a table keyed by (tenant, value_hash), and a payload that does not hash to its key is refused on read. Large text spills to a text artifact identified by length and digest; documents can be content-addressed references.

Test and Run are the two run modes. Test is a dry run: the same compiled, pinned artifact on the same execution path, with the external-write, notification and knowledge-commit sinks replaced by sinks that return a `dry-run:` receipt and send nothing; the Test opens no knowledge store. Reads and model calls in a Test are real (unless a fixture feeds it). The intended write is recoverable from the Test's journal.
claims.note: Decision D97.

claims.claim: A completed Test can be escalated into a Run. The new Run executes under the Test's pin and its journal is seeded with the Test's read and compute receipts, so only the withheld effects (writes, notifications, commits) dispatch for real. Escalation is refused if the flow changed, if the Test was fixture-fed, if the Test is not complete, or if the workspace's locality enforcement changed since the Test. The web UI exposes Escalate on a complete Test.
claims.note: This is the closest built thing to 'what I reviewed is what ran': the model output approved in Test is the output the Run writes.

claims.claim: Interrupted and parked runs continue by replay: Resume clears a pause or parked wait; Recover rebuilds from the journal after a dead process under the stored pin. Runs left `running` by a dead server are offered for explicit recovery at startup. Resume re-runs full authorisation for the starter as of now; a starter who lost authority leaves the run parked with `resume_refused: starter_unauthorized`.

Fixtures exist: a named, per-flow record of the Source inputs (file reads, document reads, URL reads) a Test should read instead of the real filesystem, document store or network, with a SHA-256 content hash. A fixture-fed Test reads only from the fixture; a read the fixture lacks is a typed `source.not_in_fixture` failure, never a fall-through to the real source. Only a Test may take a fixture. A restart refuses if the fixture's hash moved.
claims.note: Server routes exist; I found no call to the fixture/snapshot/coverage routes in web/src/features, so treat as API-level, not a confirmed UI feature.

claims.claim: Run-to-run comparison exists only as snapshot baselines for fixture runs: a completed fixture-fed Test can be accepted as the baseline for that fixture, and every later run of the same fixture reports `none`, `match` or `mismatch` with a per-terminal diff. The comparison covers the run's status and terminal outputs only. A fixture suite route runs every fixture of a flow and returns one `pass` flag; a coverage route reports which Branch arms the fixtures exercised at the current flow revision.
claims.note: Because model calls in a fixture-fed Test are live, a baseline mismatch can come from model variance as well as from a flow change. There is no general 'diff any run against any other run' route and no per-step diff.

claims.claim: There is no route that re-executes a finished run from scratch on its recorded inputs, and none that re-executes a run with model outputs substituted from an earlier run's receipts (other than Test-to-Run escalation). Starting a flow again is a new run that reads sources and calls models afresh.

claims.claim: Model nondeterminism is handled by recording, not by assuming determinism. The ruled model: pure computations (Transforms) re-run deterministically over pinned inputs; anything that cannot be deterministic (model calls, agent turns, review decisions) is an effect with a receipt; replay returns the receipt and never re-dispatches. Output generated afresh is new output with a new identity and is reviewed again rather than inheriting an earlier approval.
claims.note: No code pins temperature or seed to make a model call repeatable; I found none in flow-exec, flow-blocks or flow_source.

claims.claim: Failures are values, not dropped work. An occurrence's terminal outcome is `Value`, `Failed(causes)` or `Absent(cause)`: not-run is `Absent` with a reason (upstream failure carrying the originating node path, unselected branch arm, missing binding, erased), never a manufactured failure or a manufactured empty. A fan-in keeps all contributing causes. Failure codes are typed: Block, OperationMismatch, Uncertain, Admission, Budget, Authority, Journal, Locality.
claims.note: Semantics are stable; the names are being replaced. Ruled 2026-11-16 (v3 section 5, F114.11, not built): `Outcome<T>` becomes `Result<T>` with `Error { Failed, Blocked, Skipped }`. ops/planning/central-concepts.md:108-117.

claims.claim: In row-wise work a failed row stays in the table as a failed cell. A failed Replicate run is a failed cell of its own row and the Replicate still succeeds; a Model field whose quote cannot be verified is a failed field of a kept record; a Quote proposal that is not an exact substring is a kept row with failed cells. A committed revision that contains failed, missing or unavailable cells is marked `partial`.
claims.note: One ruled exception coming with F114.11 (not built): `?` in a function's returned expression drops the row, marked, never silent.

claims.claim: The run read serves per-node outcomes from the journal (`path, status, code, message, reason`, failed first) so the node that failed in the middle of a chain is named, rather than only a terminal that 'did not run'.

Every wire has a statically computed origin: Sourced (from a source, pasted text or a person), Computed (a pure transform of sourced inputs), Generated (a model is anywhere in the lineage; sticky through transforms, templates and Map), Verified (a Generated value checked deterministically against a Sourced one), Reviewed (a person approved it). The checker computes it from block declarations alone, and the run record reports the origin of every root output port.
claims.note: The five origins and 'Generated is sticky' are ruled (D139). Several cells of the join table are interim with open questions for the user (how Verified/Reviewed mix with other origins): origin.rs:51-63,84-87. Origins inside Jig bodies and modules are not served on the run record.

claims.claim: Only two things clear a Generated value: a deterministic check against a Sourced reference (yields Verified) and a person's approval at a HumanReview gate (yields Reviewed). In code today the Verified discharge happens only through a quote check; schema, hash and predicate checks never discharge.

The rule that committing to knowledge requires Verified or Reviewed data (an undischarged Generated value is refused) is ruled (D139) and implemented as a checker pass, but no production block declares the floor, so it does not refuse anything today.

claims.claim: Check is four deterministic, model-free blocks: CheckSchema (validates a table against a declared struct; mismatch is a hard typed failure), CheckQuote (true only if a span is an exact substring of the source text, with offsets), CheckHash (true when the SHA-256 of the input equals a pinned digest), CheckPredicate (evaluates a configured expression over a record). Each writes a write-once receipt recording block and version, mode, result, whether it discharged to Verified, and the mode's facts (offsets and anchor, digest, struct and version).

Human review is output-bound. An approval is keyed on (flow, content identity of the reviewed output, behavioural provenance: producing block and version, prompt revision, settings, upstream settled frontier, authority digest), so an approval of one output cannot cover an identical sentence produced from different inputs. A settled review is a receipt: replay returns the recorded decision and does not re-ask. Review cadence is a policy, `Always | OnChange | Off`, default `OnChange`. A run parks durably while a review is outstanding.
claims.note: The frontier and authority digests are provisional definitions (SPEC_GAP in review_subject.rs:11-13); upstream input content identities are not yet folded into provenance (host.rs:642-643). `Once` was dropped from the policy (D90 #2).

claims.claim: Gates that exist in code: (1) HumanReview on an output; (2) revision approval before a Run, opt-in per tenant with levels Off (default), Unattended (host-started runs and agent-started runs need an approved revision) and AllRuns, stored per (tenant, flow, revision) and reported stale when the review key moves; a Test is never gated; (3) Declassify releases that lower a data label, registered only by a person who owns the flow or tenant, bound to a digest of everything upstream, and requiring human review every time when the redactor is model-based; (4) budget and resource-limit parks that pause a run for a raise/fail decision; (5) the locality check, which refuses or records a crossing depending on the tenant's `enforce_locality`.
claims.note: Product stance is that friction is opt-in: gates are built but ship off by default (central-concepts.md:198-212). Gate defaults were re-ruled as recently as 2026-11-15/16 (ops/agent-drift/2026-11-15 - Admission and Approval Gates as Defaults.md; 2026-11-16 - Gate Policy...). Whether Notify is approval-gated is an open policy question (host.rs:826-828). The composition-level authority screen currently passes every subject (host.rs:736-760).

claims.claim: Commit turns a completed run table into an immutable knowledge revision in one SQLite transaction in the tenant's knowledge-table store, separate from the run's store, so it outlives the run. The commit joins the labels of the table, rows and cells, writes a snapshot under a knowledge identity, and pins every outcome, carried cell and nested table the snapshot depends on so garbage collection cannot break it. A revision can be a set of several named tables committed together: all members or none.
claims.note: 'Commit set' is the code's name for the multi-table revision (commit.rs:95-109).

claims.claim: What a knowledge commit refuses today: a table that is not Complete; a source revision that moved since the caller read it (typed conflict, never auto-merged); a `replaces` revision that never existed; a cell whose referent is gone; an empty set, duplicate or invalid member names; a hand edit with no recorded actor, base revision or op digest; a commit whose authority was revoked (rechecked inside the transaction); a run with no person to check the commit permission against; and a host-started (unattended) run. A stale `replaces` is accepted as a fork with both heads kept. The same source revision under the same identity is idempotent.
claims.note: Who commits for an agent-credential or trigger-started run is an explicit open policy question (sinks.rs:199-212); refused until ruled.

claims.claim: A flow reads committed knowledge as a pinned revision: a `TableSource::pinned` occurrence copies the revision from the tenant store into the run store with cells materialised to verified payloads, keeping `value_hash` and cell labels. A revision with cells that are not succeeded (a partial revision) cannot be imported.

claims.claim: Retention default is keep everything: nothing is deleted silently, garbage collection is off unless an owner turns it on, and when on it removes only unreferenced outcomes; committed revisions are never collected. vocabulary_current: Run: one execution of a flow, in mode `test` or `run`, with its own journal and stores
Test: a dry run of the same pinned artifact; writes, notifications and knowledge commits are replaced by no-op sinks
Run (mode): an execution whose external writes and commits are persisted
Escalate: turn a completed Test into a Run under the same pin, reusing the Test's receipts
Resume / Recover: continue a parked run / rebuild an interrupted run from its journal
Journal: the per-run, per-occurrence durable record that is the replay authority
Receipt: the durable record of one non-deterministic effect; also the opaque text an external write returns (`WriteReceipt`)
Sub-receipt: a write-once record of a model step, tool call, refusal or deterministic check beneath a block occurrence
Occurrence / NodePath: one execution instance of a node, identified by node id plus row / round / call-site
Request fingerprint: SHA-256 identity of (block, resolved config, canonical input[, prompt regime]) checked on replay
Pin / pinned run definition (RunDefinition): the immutable definition a run executes
Compile key: content hash of the compiled artifact
Source revision: hash of the flow source a run started from
ir_hash: span-free hash of the flow's meaning
Outcome: Value | Failed | Absent (current code name; being replaced by Result)
Uncertain: an effect dispatched with no recorded result; never blindly repeated
OperationMismatch: a replay whose request differs from the saved one
Parked: a run waiting durably on a review, timer, rate limit, budget or limit
Fixture: a named, hashed record of Source inputs a Test reads instead of the real sources
Snapshot baseline: an accepted fixture-run result later runs of that fixture are diffed against
Fixture suite / coverage: run every fixture as a Test; report which Branch arms were exercised
Origin: Sourced, Computed, Generated, Verified, Reviewed
Discharge: moving a Generated value to Verified (deterministic check) or Reviewed (person)
Origin floor: the minimum origin a destination requires (only KnowledgeCommit is defined; not yet declared in production)
Check: the four deterministic blocks CheckSchema, CheckQuote, CheckHash, CheckPredicate
Quote / Anchor: a verbatim span of a source document and its resolvable location
HumanReview / Review: the output-bound human gate
ReviewPolicy: Always | OnChange | Off
Revision approval: opt-in gate requiring an approved flow revision before a Run (Off | Unattended | AllRuns)
Declassify / release: the owner-registered path that lowers a data label
Label / Locality / crossing: data sensitivity label, where data may go, and a recorded instance of data leaving its ring
Knowledge base / knowledge revision: Functionary's store of tables and documents; an immutable committed revision
Commit / commit set: promote a completed run table (or several named tables atomically) to a knowledge revision
Block: trusted implementation agents configure but do not rewrite
Jig: visible loop/control construct (Map, Repeat, Refine, Retry, Replicate)
Model block: fills a declared struct from text with a verified quote per field

truth.summary: Functionary has two distinct kinds of agent, bounded differently. The authoring agent (code name "project agent") writes and revises flows through a closed, allowlisted set of server-side tools; it has no shell or filesystem tool, its flow changes are typed edit ops that must pass the checker, and it gets run tools (start, read, cancel, read-transcript) only when a person starts a turn in auto mode. Auto mode (F111, landed on bleeding 2026-11-15 to 11-17) is an author-run-read-revise loop with mechanical stop rules decided server-side; it is permissive by default (real runs, full output content) with two lock-down settings (auto_run_scope, auto_read_scope) that an organisation sets and a session may only narrow. The Agent block is an inner agent inside a flow: a closed five-tool vocabulary (call_block over four allowlisted blocks, three knowledge-table tools, bash), with bash in a per-run bwrap sandbox with fresh scratch, network off by default, a program allowlist, and wall/scratch/step limits; it cannot call Jigs, egress blocks, Review or another Agent, and it never falls back to an unconfined process. Locality is a four-ring label (LocalOnly < Controlled < Region < Anywhere) computed and propagated on every value; since the 2026-11-15 ruling it is enforced only when the tenant's enforce_locality policy is on (off for Personal, on for Governed), and otherwise each crossing is recorded durably per run and reported by the checker as a note. Model connections come in seven kinds (claude_cli, codex_cli, anthropic_api, openai_api, openrouter, custom_endpoint, ollama); inner agents accept only the API kinds, excluded by type. Reach to the outside world today is narrower than the planning record suggests: sources are FileSource, FolderSource, UrlSource, DocumentSource and TableSource; egress is Write (granted files, model-draft), KnowledgeWrite and Notify; the 20-odd service integrations (Gmail, Slack, Jira, ...) have compiled readers but no flow block calls them, Notify has no email/chat/push adapter, and Search's web mode is not runnable. Browser use (F118) is a spec plus an out-of-repo spike, explicitly deprioritized. What I could not find is a client surface that renders a run's recorded crossings to the person: the server route exists and the authoring agent sees them, but neither web/src nor fnary reads it.

claims.claim: The authoring agent is one server-side agent (code name project_agent) that converses about a project and authors flows only through a typed, allowlisted tool registry. A tool outside the allowlist returns a typed NotPermitted denial and is never executed.
claims.note: Internal identifier is still project_agent; ops docs call it the authoring agent.

claims.claim: The authoring agent's full tool set is: 4 project reads (get_project_overview, kb_search, kb_read, list_effective_filesystem_roots), 3 project writes (set_flow_project, create_project, update_project), ask_user, 8 flow-authoring tools (restricted_list_flows, create_flow, read_flow, edit_flow, check_flow, rename_flow, read_layout, arrange_flow), and in auto mode 4 run tools. There is no shell, file-write or arbitrary-code tool, and delete_project, delete_flow, publish_module and run_flow are absent from the schema.
claims.note: The bound is structural (the tool list), not a prompt instruction.

claims.claim: The authoring agent cannot edit a flow outside the flow language. A flow is created from source that the checker must admit, and edited by typed source ops (insert_block, set_option, set_mode, set_expression, remove_block) plus config members, applied all-or-nothing. The checker is CST -> fail-closed screen -> IR derivation -> declaration-driven contract check.
claims.note: Flow source is an allowlisted Rust subset (per 2026-11-15 Agent Mode Equivalence doc section 6); the surface syntax itself is in flux under the 2026-11-16 v3 flow-language rulings.

claims.claim: The authoring agent acts under a server-minted, short-lived (120 s) agent credential bound to the signed-in person and tenant. The restricted backend itself refuses an agent credential for Credential-class setting writes (including runtime limits such as max_steps), review answers and commits; there is no tool for a review answer or commit in any mode.
claims.note: Enforced by the routes' policy on the credential class, not by the prompt.

claims.claim: Outside auto mode the authoring agent cannot start or read a run: the run tools are not offered and a call to one is refused before any request is sent.
claims.note: Supersedes the earlier position 'the authoring agent deliberately has no run tool' (withdrawn by the 2026-11-15 locality ruling doc, 'What this corrects').

claims.claim: Auto mode is a turn a person starts with auto: true and a goal. The agent authors, runs, reads the result and revises until it proposes done or a stop rule fires. Stop rules are decided server-side from run-tool results, not from the model's own count: run cap (default 5 per turn), repeated identical failure (default 2 revisions), a run parked on a person (review, budget/limit raise, pause), a tenant policy refusal, and the spend limit.
claims.note: Shape is stable; default numbers are env-tunable constants and the 'who judges the goal met' question is listed open in the F111 plan section 5.

claims.claim: In auto mode the agent may start real runs (writes, notifications and knowledge commits happen) or Test runs (dry run, nothing leaves the run), read status, per-node outcomes, output content (16 KB per output, 64 KB total per read) and the run's locality crossings, and cancel a run.
claims.note: Permissive default is a 2026-11-15 user ruling (F111 plan section 2 #2).

claims.claim: Two lock-down settings bound auto mode: auto_run_scope (runs | test_only | none) and auto_read_scope (content | status_only). Both default to the permissive value. They live on the tenant governance policy; a session can override them from fnary (--auto-runs, --auto-reads, /limits), but a member of a Governed tenant may only narrow, not widen.
claims.note: Landed 2026-11-16/17; fix commits still arriving.

claims.claim: Authority to start a real run is scoped to the auto-mode session: an auto-mode turn's credential carries a signed run grant that the run policy honours in a Personal tenant; a Governed tenant must additionally turn on agent_runs (default off).
claims.note: 0c85652b reverted an earlier change that made agent_runs default on for Personal; the session grant replaced it.

claims.claim: A run that parks on a person (Review gate, budget raise) ends the auto turn; only the person can answer, with their own sign-in. fnary lets the person answer inline (/review, /budget) and optionally tells the agent to carry on.
claims.note: A run parked on human input (not review/budget) still has to be answered in the canvas Runs view.

claims.claim: The authoring agent reads an Agent block's inner transcript only under a per-block permission that a person turns on; it is off by default, off again for a block added or renamed since, and a refused read returns 403. Reads are paged (10 steps default, 50 max, 64 KB cap).
claims.note: Landed 2026-11-17. cli/fnary/README.md:141 still says none of the transcript is sent to the authoring agent, which predates this permission.

claims.claim: The Agent block (Agent@v1, kind Agent) is an inner agent placed as one step in a flow. It accepts any wired inputs and returns one Text output with origin Generated, labelled with the join of every input label and every granted table read.

The Agent block's tool vocabulary is a closed enum of five tools: call_block, list_knowledge_tables, read_knowledge_page, open_knowledge_table, bash. Every call carries a required stated reason (1-400 chars) that is journaled as context and never treated as true.
claims.note: The crate's header comment (lib.rs:12) still says 'one tool'; the enum below it has five.

claims.claim: Blocks callable as Agent tools today are four: FileSource, DocumentSource, Summarize, Template. The allowlist is built before the session exists and refuses a Jig, an effect-bearing block (Write, KnowledgeWrite, HumanReview/Review), another Agent, an unknown block, and anything without a dispatch adapter (UrlSource, Search, TableSource, Judge, Coalesce are refused as NoAdapter). At most 16 tools per step.
claims.note: The refusal classes are stable; the set of four is expected to grow 'as adapters land' (F101.147 decision 6).

claims.claim: Agent bash runs in an OS sandbox (bubblewrap namespaces, seccomp syscall denylist, read-only root, cleared environment, prlimit caps). Each run gets a new scratch directory that is deleted when the run ends. If the sandbox cannot be built the step is refused; there is no unconfined fallback.
claims.note: D169 superseded D168 #2: OS sandbox now, microVM later (decisions.md:3220-3228).

claims.claim: Agent block sandbox isolation is Linux-only today (bwrap). A second Linux engine (Landlock) exists in the isolation crate; macOS Seatbelt and a microVM engine are named follow-ups behind the same runner trait.
claims.note: Cross-platform release is epic F112, actively moving.

claims.claim: Agent block settings and defaults: bash on, network off, programs = default allowlist, show_goal on, show_flow_source on, max_steps 40, timeout 10 minutes (max 24 h), scratch 256 MB (max 4 GiB), optional max_spend, a required data ceiling, a required Models connection. Every field is visible and classed as behaviour, so a change invalidates review.
claims.note: Defaults are D168 #5 rulings; the maxima are marked SPEC_GAP (agent-chosen bounds).

claims.claim: Network inside the Agent sandbox is Off (private loopback only) or On, where On is the unfiltered host network including host loopback services, with no guardrails. The sandbox mounts none of /etc, so with network on there is no DNS resolver config or CA bundle.
claims.note: D168 #3 requires the editor to warn that network-on is unsafe; I found no such warning string in web/src. A proxy-only mode (F118.8) is proposed in the browser spec and not built.

claims.claim: The Agent bash program list is either a default allowlist (jq, yq, awk, sed, pandoc, csvkit tools, sh, bash and ~20 coreutils) or 'all' (every program under the host's system directories, mounted read-only). The code states the allowlist bounds what the shell finds by name and is not a security boundary; the boundary is the namespaces, syscall filter and empty filesystem.
claims.note: The exact coreutils list is marked SPEC_GAP (agent proposal).

claims.claim: Data enters the Agent sandbox only as wired inputs, written read-only at /ro/in/<port>.txt, plus optionally the flow goal at /ro/ctx/goal.md. The agent's output is /scratch/response.md, read back as the block's Text output.
claims.note: Paths differ from the 2026-11-06 proposal (/in, /ctx, /work, /out); the code layout is authoritative.

claims.claim: Each Agent tool call is journaled as a sub-receipt under the step; a resumed or replayed run applies the recorded effects without dispatching the block or re-running bash. The recorded trace can be stabilized into an ordinary checked flow; the trace is read, never executed.
claims.note: Per D168 #7, turning bash steps into blocks is a manual coding task, not automatic.

claims.claim: Effects inside an Agent block (letting the agent itself call Write or Notify) are not available; all sending happens in egress blocks wired after the agent. Allowing it later by a per-destination setting is ruled but not built.
claims.note: The refusal is built; the future opt-in is the DECIDED part.

claims.claim: Inner agents (Agent and Search blocks) run on a Functionary-owned loop and may use only API model endpoints: openrouter, openai_api, anthropic_api, custom_endpoint. CLI connections (claude_cli, codex_cli) are refused because they carry their own tools, and the exclusion is by type: no constructor takes an arbitrary provider. Ollama connections are refused for inner agents unless saved as a custom endpoint at its /v1 URL.
claims.note: D61. The browser spec notes its external-driver ruling needs reconciling with D61 (F118.6).

claims.claim: A saved Models connection is one of seven kinds: claude_cli, codex_cli, anthropic_api, openai_api, openrouter, custom_endpoint, ollama. The CLI kinds authenticate through a local Claude or Codex subscription login and use no API key.
claims.note: LocalBackend also reserves vLLM and llama.cpp; only Ollama is wired (config.rs:85-93). Credential sources: env var and inline only; keychain and vault are reserved.

claims.claim: An inner agent's model connection is re-checked with the server immediately before every live model call; a connection disabled, a model removed, a policy narrowed or an endpoint edited mid-session refuses the next step. There is no quota fallback to another model.

Locality is a four-ring label on every value: LocalOnly < Controlled < Region(R) < Anywhere. Content read from a local file, document or table is labelled local-only, and labels propagate to derived values and receipts. A model endpoint's placement maps onto the same ring: loopback = LocalOnly, a tenant host = Controlled, a vendor = Anywhere.
claims.note: Controlled and Region admit nothing beyond this machine yet: tenant attestation (F98.17) is not built (provider.rs:92-100).

claims.claim: Locality enforcement is a tenant policy (enforce_locality): off by default for a Personal tenant, on for a Governed tenant. Off, a value whose label does not admit a destination still goes there, the run records the crossing and the checker reports a locality_crossing note. On, the checker refuses the flow and the run refuses the step.
claims.note: 2026-11-15 user ruling. Supersedes 'a local file's content may not leave the machine until a declassifier says otherwise' as a default, and D37's hard ceiling read as unconditional. Still open per the ruling doc: who may release a label when enforcing, the Agent/Search ceiling default, the final form of the crossing record.

claims.claim: A locality crossing record names the node path, the block, the kind (input, placement, web, knowledge), the reach the data admitted and where it went; it names no value. Crossings are appended to a durable per-run file and served by GET /api/restricted-backend/flows/{id}/runs/{run}/crossings to anyone who may view the flow.
claims.note: The record's form is marked SPEC_GAP pending the user's ruling.

claims.claim: Redact and Declassify are the gates that lower a locality label. Redact lowers its approved output to Anywhere, and the checker and the run agree on this.

How the person sees what leaves the machine today: (1) the checker's locality_crossing note on the flow, (2) a workspace governance toggle 'Enforce where data may go' with an explanation, (3) the data-ceiling picker on the Agent and Search cards, (4) the live run transcript. I found no web or fnary code that reads or renders a run's recorded crossings list.

truth.summary: Nothing is downloadable today: the repo tjmisko/Functionary is PRIVATE, has no license (GitHub licenseInfo null; Cargo license is the placeholder `LicenseRef-Functionary-Placeholder`), has zero GitHub releases, and `release.yml` only validates a nightly tag and fast-forwards `main` -- it builds no artifacts. The release work is epic F112 (Linux + platform-neutral), split on 2026-11-16 into F119 (macOS) and F120 (Windows), each gated by a fresh-machine walk; F119 and F120 depend on the Linux gate F112.0. As of 2026-11-17 roughly half of F112's own tasks are merged to `bleeding` (loopback bind, persisted first-run keys, build identity and /api/version, data-format stamp, migration registry, pre-migration snapshots, graceful shutdown, isolation seam, interpreter crate, release profile), but every user-facing delivery piece is still open: the launcher `functionary start`, the embedded UI (in review, not merged), the first-run owner account, the prebuilt flow runner, the updater, the versioned install layout, the release job, archives, packages and signing. Every F119 and F120 task is open or blocked, so macOS and Windows are planned targets with no shipped work beyond compile-gating. Today the product only starts from a source checkout via `scripts/run.sh` (bash 4.3+, Rust toolchain, Node), and running a flow still needs `rustc`, a system linker and `bwrap`/`prlimit` on the host; the interpreter that removes this exists as a crate but is not wired into the server. A hosted cloud service is user direction in a 2026-11-14 draft only (stateless replicas over Postgres and object storage); none of it is built, and whether binary or hosted ships first is an open question. Personal vs organization tenants and Personal vs Governed access policy are built and structurally stable; organization creation is behind an off-by-default env flag. `fnary` is a working Node/TypeScript terminal client for the project agent, private and unpublished, with distribution and whether it ships in the installer both unruled. No release date exists anywhere in the record; the only milestone definition is the gate walk.

truth.summary: Functionary today is a browser UI (React 18 + Vite, React Flow canvas) talking to a local Rust server, plus a terminal client `fnary`; on `bleeding` (7f74919d, 2026-11-17) it is still started as a dev stack by `scripts/run.sh` (backend :3001, Vite :5173). There is no desktop app and no downloadable binary yet: the single-binary local product (embedded UI, `functionary start` launcher, first-run account, prebuilt flow runner, updater, release archives) is epic F112, about half merged, with the embedded-UI task in review and the launcher, release job and epic gate still open; macOS (F119) and Windows (F120) are separate later phases. The UI is organised as Projects -> a project workspace (Overview, Flows, Planning, Data, Runs, plus Monitoring/Security/Models) -> a flow with three views (Editor, Data, Runs), with a project Agent drawer docked on the right across all of them and a `:` command palette. The editor canvas is a projection of checked Rust-subset flow source: every edit is a semantic op posted to the server, there is no local save. Runs have two modes, Test and Run, with Pause/Resume/Recover/Escalate, a run panel (Needs you, Steps, Limits, Results) and review forms for runs parked on a person; revision approval ("strict mode") gates Run on an approved revision. The canvas node visual language was redesigned 2026-11-13 and landed within days (per-type node faces with in-place editable fields), but the record itself says "locked for a first implementation; the user expects more iteration", many node types are Provisional or Open, and the flow language rulings of 2026-11-16 (v3) rename and remove blocks, so any depiction of specific nodes is unsafe. `fnary` is the fastest-moving surface (epic F111, landing daily): chat, auto mode, a project as a directory of `flow.rs` files, run transcripts and review answering from the terminal. The stable things to describe in words are structural: flow-as-source projected to a canvas, Test vs Run with Escalate, wires that carry value origin, people-only review and revision approval, and the web/terminal pair over one server.

audits.summary:
Audit of ~/Projects/functionary-site/src/pages/index.astro plus KnowledgeWorkHero, Canvas, FlowSource, Refusal, RunTable, Kinds and lib/{flows,flow,canvas}.ts against the ground-truth record, with three spot checks in ~/Projects/Functionary (trigger dispatch, knowledge origin floor, site page list).

What survives (prose, structural, low staleness): the H1 and the "mechanical research tasks" section; the problem statement (a chat answer hides the work; one unvetted source spoils the deliverable); model-written values stay marked Generated until a deterministic check against a source or a person clears them; canvas is derived from source and canvas edits write back to source; the checker refuses improvised loops and side I/O (fail closed); blocks do one bounded job and the model inside cannot exceed it; every model call leaves a receipt; failures stay as failed rows; Test withholds writes; the seven kinds; the five origins; iterate-then-stabilize with opt-in controls (pins, approved revision before unattended runs); runs, receipts and results live under one local data directory.

What must go (every diagram and mock UI): the hero mock (chat, canvas, run summary, preview table), both Provenance canvases, the canvas/source bijection, the flow snippet, the Refusal figure, the run table mock, and the per-kind verb table. All imitate surfaces that are mid-redesign (canvas node language "locked for a first implementation", run panel a WIP checkpoint, flow language re-ruled 2026-11-16 with F110 unmerged and F114 unbuilt). The snippet names two blocks that do not exist (Field, Source::new) and is wrong on bleeding, on integrate/f110 and after F114.

Outright false or unbuilt claims in prose: "The knowledge base refuses anything nobody cleared" (origin floor is implemented in the checker but no production declaration carries it); "Functionary is a desktop tool" (it is a local server with a browser UI and a terminal client, fnary); "Start it on a schedule, a webhook or an inbound email" (trigger intake exists, but dispatch to the current run route is not wired: crates/functionary-server/src/legacy_retirement.rs:308-318; only a manual fire route); "The diagnostic names the step to use instead" (bleeding emits a code, construct and span; prose guidance is ruled, not built); "Nothing was saved / canvas keeps the last accepted flow" (incomplete drafts are savable); the Deployment CTA to /self-hosting (no release, no license, private repo); Egress verb Apply (not declared); Notify shown messaging recipients (no sender adapter exists); Search "web" mode (not runnable); Replicate "3 runs, 3 models" (declared diversity retired).

Vocabulary to change everywhere: step -> block / block call; Sketch agent -> Agent; `Source` as a block name -> the Source kind (FileSource, UrlSource, ...); Row/Record wire types retired.

Gaps against the intended framing (nothing on the page today): the reproduce-to-trust argument is absent; the page says "provenance" but never says why a declared, pinned, recorded process is what makes agent work checkable. The built substrate to draw on is stable: runs pinned to an exact flow revision, settings and block versions; every effect recorded as a receipt and replayed from the record rather than re-called; Test escalated to Run so the reviewed output is the output written; review approvals bound to the output they covered. Wording caution: no route re-executes a finished run or diffs two runs, and nothing claims identical model output on re-run, so "reproduce" should mean "the process is a fixed program and the record of each run is complete", not "one-click replay". Also absent: the terminal client and auto mode (now co-equal with the canvas in ops), and any download shell. The CTA section ("Where it runs") is the natural place for the download shell; it can state local-first, one data directory, no telemetry by default, and name no platform, version, license, install command or date.

Unresolved for the user: whether "technical tool" means the fnary/coding-agent audience (ops archetype doc still says the Associate never reads source); how strong "reproduce" is allowed to be; and whether /how-it-works (outside this audit, but linked from the CTA and containing Judge::new / Check::new snippets and the checkCitations, sourceValidation and bestOfN canvases) is kept.

items.text: Agent Harness for Knowledge Work
items.reason: Matches the requested framing exactly. 'Harness' is not an ops term for the product (only for the fnary terminal harness and test harnesses), so the site is the first place it is used; that is the user's call and it is made.

items.text: Give agents the work of gathering sources, checking references, and assembling data. Functionary turns that work into a flow you can inspect and run, with each result linked to its sources.
items.reason: First sentence and 'a flow you can inspect and run' are built and structural. 'Each result linked to its sources' overclaims: origin is tracked per wire and Model/Quote record a verified quote per field, but Quote/Anchor source-span ties (F104.15) and the Verified producer are open, and origins are served for root output ports only. The lead also omits the reason to reach for the tool (reproduce to trust).
items.suggested_fact: The agent writes the work as a program (a flow) built only from pre-built blocks; a conventional runtime executes it, every run is pinned to the exact flow revision and settings, and every model call and external effect is recorded. That record is what lets a person check the work instead of redoing it.
items.evidence: Ground truth: identity core mechanism (BUILT, stable); provenance claim note (F104.10/F104.15 open); runs: origins 'reported for root output ports only'.

items.text: <KnowledgeWorkHero /> embedded as the hero figure
items.reason: A mock of chat, canvas, run panel and result table. Each surface it imitates is in flux (canvas node design, run panel WIP checkpoint, block names under v3 rulings). The user asked to drop it. Itemised below under KnowledgeWorkHero.astro.

items.text: Functionary is a desktop tool. The canvas is best read on a larger screen.
items.reason: Not a desktop application: a local Rust server with a browser UI (React + Vite) and a terminal client; no Electron/Tauri shell. The second sentence only exists to excuse the embedded canvas.
items.suggested_fact: Functionary runs as a local server on your machine with a browser interface and a terminal client.
items.evidence: Ground truth surfaces: 'There is no desktop-app shell (no Electron/Tauri) in the repo' (web/src/App.tsx, README.md:8).

items.text: Automate Mechanical Research Tasks
items.reason: Fits 'the mechanical parts of knowledge work', which is the stable phrase in the repo README and AGENTS.md. 'Research' is narrower than 'knowledge work' but consistent with the task list.

items.text: Much of the time spent on research goes to moving and organizing information: opening documents, finding passages, copying figures, checking references, and filling in tables. These jobs repeat those steps across dozens or hundreds of sources.
items.reason: Describes the work, not the product. Matches the 2026-10-19 author's account (tasks of dozens to hundreds of steps, none hard alone).

items.text: Task cards: Report QC; Dataset Assembly; Evidence Collection (with their descriptions)
items.reason: These are the recorded target uses (QC of a work product against its sources; building a model from filings; combing a document set for evidence and counterevidence). They are intended uses: example flows for them do not exist as a product surface. Present as the kind of work it is for, not as shipped templates.

items.reason: 'Sourcing and cleaning data against criteria' is a recorded target use, but 'gather sources on a topic' implies web search. Search's web mode is not runnable; today sources are granted files and folders, URLs, documents and knowledge tables.

items.reason: A form of 'secondary market research', a recorded target use; expressible as Map over a table with Model and table verbs. Intended use, not a shipped example.

items.reason: Not among the recorded target uses and nothing in the record produces a redline. The only document output paths are Write (file or model draft) and KnowledgeWrite. Keeping it implies a capability nobody has verified.
items.evidence: Ground truth egress claim: Write, KnowledgeWrite, Notify only; Apply (ChangeSet) not declared.

items.text: Provenance
items.reason: The section holds the trust argument but the heading names a mechanism. Per the brief the header should carry the reason: you have to be able to reproduce (check) an agent's work to trust it. Provenance is one of the means.

items.text: A chat assistant gives you an answer. It does not give you the work behind it. In research, one unvetted source or skipped step spoils the deliverable, and nothing in the finished output shows where.
items.reason: This is the recorded problem statement (transcript, not a declared process; a skipped step or unvetted source contaminates silently). It is the opening for the reproduce-to-trust argument and should be extended to say so: today the only way to trust the answer is to redo the work.

items.text: Functionary shows every step that ran.
items.reason: True in substance: a durable per-run journal with one entry per block occurrence and per-node outcomes served on the run read. 'Step' is retired vocabulary (ruled 2026-11-16: block call). Known gaps (Retry deletes failed-attempt rows; live transcripts are ephemeral) do not contradict the sentence at this level.
items.suggested_fact: Every block call in a run is recorded: what it was asked, with which settings, and what it returned.

items.text: A value a model wrote stays marked until a check against the source or a person clears it.
items.reason: Origin is computed statically for every wire; Generated is sticky through transforms, Template and Map; Verified (deterministic quote check against a sourced value) and Reviewed (a person) are the only discharges. Ruled in D139 and unchanged by v3. Some join-table cells are interim but the sentence does not depend on them.

items.text: The knowledge base refuses anything nobody cleared.
items.reason: Not true today. The origin-floor pass exists in the checker but no production declaration carries a floor, so nothing is refused. Whether Sourced/Computed values meet the floor is also unruled.
items.evidence: crates/functionary-flow-check/src/origin.rs:111-139,248-255 ('No production declaration carries a floor until F104.12'); I confirmed crates/functionary-flow-contract/src/lib.rs:2070,2088 declare origin_floor: None.

items.text: Canvas figure (flow 'unchecked') with caption: A model-written table heads for the knowledge base. The dashed wire says a model wrote it, and the Write refuses it.
items.reason: Depicts a refusal that is not enforced (see origin floor). The dashed-wire styling is the site's own: the product's edge currently carries origin as a class/title only. Node faces are mid-redesign.

items.text: Canvas figure (flow 'checked') with caption: A Check confirms each quote is in the filing. The wire after it is verified, and the Write accepts it.
items.reason: The fact is real and worth keeping in prose: CheckQuote is true only when the span is an exact substring of the source, and that is the one check that discharges Generated to Verified. The drawing imitates in-flux node faces, and 'the Write accepts it' implies the unenforced floor.
items.suggested_fact: A deterministic check can confirm that a quoted passage is an exact substring of the source document; a value that passes is marked Verified rather than Generated.

items.text: Canvas and source
items.reason: Leads with the canvas. Since 2026-11-15 the ops centre of gravity is 'agents write understandable programs that do your work', with the terminal as the familiar way in and the canvas as the review surface. For a technical-tool framing the header should be about the program being the thing that runs.
items.evidence: ops/planning/2026-11-15 - Agent Mode Equivalence and Headless Fnary.md:9-19,32-35.

items.text: The agent writes the flow as steps.
items.reason: Underlying point is the core mechanism, but 'steps' is retired and the sentence undersells it: the agent writes a program in a restricted, statically checked subset of Rust that can only wire together pre-built blocks; it implements no algorithm and a conventional runtime, not the agent, executes it.
items.suggested_fact: The agent writes the flow as a small program that can only wire together pre-built blocks. It chooses blocks, sets their settings and connects outputs to inputs. A conventional runtime runs it; the agent does not.

items.text: The canvas is drawn from what it wrote, and an edit on the canvas goes back into it.
items.reason: Source is canonical; the canvas is a derived projection; canvas edits are semantic ops applied as minimal source diffs under a tested isomorphism. 'Drawn from' is the accurate wording (not 'one-to-one': cards group blocks, transform chains collapse).

items.text: There is no hidden code.
items.reason: The real commitment is narrower and stronger: the graph is read statically from source and is the only execution model, and every loop and branch is a visible Jig. 'No hidden code' is loose: settings live outside source, block internals and prompts are Functionary's, and an Agent block can run bash. It is also a negated benefit.
items.suggested_fact: What you read is what runs: the runtime executes the graph read from the source, and every loop and branch in it is a visible construct.
items.evidence: Backend Guiding Principles P3, P7; v3 rulings :172-184.

items.text: If the agent tries to write its own loop or read a file on the side, the save is refused and the canvas keeps the last accepted flow.
items.reason: The refusal is real and structural: the screen is fail-closed and refuses for/while/loop/if, operators and non-builder calls before any graph is derived; the authoring agent also has no shell or file tool at all. 'The canvas keeps the last accepted flow' is not established: a screened-out source yields a projection with no graph plus chips, and incomplete drafts are savable.
items.suggested_fact: The checker accepts only the allowed constructs and refuses everything else, so an improvised loop or a file read outside a Source block never becomes a flow. The authoring agent has no shell or file tool to go around it.

items.text: Side-by-side figure labelled 'Canvas' and 'Source' (Canvas flow scanBody next to FlowSource scanSource)
items.reason: Implies one drawn node per source line, which is not how the projection works, and both halves use blocks that do not exist (Field, Source). Any verbatim canvas/source pair goes stale when F110 merges and again with F114.

items.reason: Flows are written as flows/<slug>/flow.rs with settings.toml, goal.md and layout.json; there is no <name>.rs per flow.

items.reason: The refusals are real; the diagnostic text is not. 'Says what to write instead' is the ruled standard (v3:25) being built on the unmerged F110 branch.

items.text: Steps
items.reason: Retired word. The ruled term is 'block' (and 'block call' for one use). The section's point for the framing is bounding: agents compose trusted blocks, and an inner agent gets a narrow job.

items.text: Each step does one job: summarize this page, grade this source against these criteria, pull the passages that bear on a question.
items.reason: Blocks are trusted, versioned units each doing one job; Summarize and Quote exist and are stable. 'Grade this source' maps to JudgeGrade, which is ruled to become a Model preset; phrased as plain-language work it survives, but avoid the block name. Replace 'step' with 'block'.
items.suggested_fact: Each block does one job: summarize this page, pull the passages that bear on a question, fill these fields from this document.

items.text: The model inside a step can only do what that step allows.
items.reason: Inner agents run inside blocks with narrow context and recorded prompts; an authoring agent may configure a block but not rewrite it or its prompts; the Agent block's tools are a closed set in a sandbox. This is the bounding claim the brief wants. Change 'step' to 'block'.

items.text: Every model call leaves a receipt.
items.reason: Each model call is a write-once sub-receipt (reply text, model name, prompt revision) under the block occurrence; every effect passes one boundary that records before a dependant proceeds. This is the substrate of the reproducibility argument and should be tied to it: a resumed or escalated run reuses the recorded result rather than calling the model again.

items.text: A page that failed to load is a failed row in the result, not a blank.
items.reason: Failures are values: a failed row stays in the table as a failed cell and not-run is recorded with a reason. The names are changing (Outcome to Result, Failed/Blocked/Skipped) but the sentence uses none of them. One ruled exception is coming (`?` drops a row, marked), which does not contradict it.

items.text: Test runs the whole flow and holds back the writes, so you read the outcome before anything leaves.
items.reason: Test is a dry run of the same pinned program with write, notify and knowledge-commit sinks replaced. 'Before anything leaves' overclaims: reads and model calls in a Test are real, so content does go to the model provider. The stronger, accurate point is Escalate: a completed Test becomes a Run under the same pin reusing the Test's recorded results, so what you reviewed is what gets written.
items.suggested_fact: Test runs the whole flow and withholds the writes and notifications. Approve it and the same recorded results are what get written; the models are not called again.

items.text: RunTable mock titled 'Weekly scan', 'Run table · Test', badge 'result', columns site / fetched / summary / receipt, with cells such as '200 · 41 KB', '403' failed, and 'sha256:9f2a1c…' per row

The real run panel (Needs you, Steps, Limits, Results) is a WIP checkpoint and is not a per-row receipt table; a 'receipt' hash column per row, an HTTP status cell and per-cell origin dots are inventions of the site. Whether any client shows a receipt browser is unverified in the record.

items.reason: Caption of the dropped mock. The fact (Map gives one output row per input row; a failed row is kept) is built and stable and can live in prose.
items.suggested_fact: A loop over a table returns one row per input row, and a row that failed is kept and marked as failed.

items.text: <Kinds /> palette with note: The seven kinds of step, and the verbs under each.
items.reason: 'Seven kinds' is correct and structurally stable (one enum in the contract crate, unchanged by v3). The verb lists under each are not: at least Coalesce, Branch-in-source and the Judge blocks are ruled to change, Apply is not built, and the count should not be printed. Keep the seven kinds as a short prose or one-line list; drop the per-kind verb table. 'Kinds of step' becomes 'kinds of block'.
items.suggested_fact: A flow is built from seven kinds of building block: Source, Block, Agent, Transform, Jig, Gate, Egress.

items.text: Iteration
items.reason: Fits progressive formalization (confirmed central 2026-11-16) and the Associate/Automator line. A value-first header would say what the reader gets (fix the process once and it stays fixed).

items.text: Describe the job and the agent drafts the flow. Test it, read every row, change a setting or delete a step, and run again.
items.reason: True of the attended loop. It omits the largest recent change: in auto mode the authoring agent itself alternates between writing the flow and running it toward a goal, from the terminal client. Auto mode is built but landing daily, so mention it at the level of the commitment only (the agent writes and runs the program; you review the program), not its limits or commands. 'Step' to 'block'.
items.suggested_fact: Describe the job. The agent writes the flow, runs it, reads the results and revises it. You read the program and the results, change a setting or remove a block, and run again.

audits.summary:
Audited /home/tjmisko/Projects/functionary-site/src/pages/how-it-works.astro plus the flow data only it uses (checkCitations, sourceValidation, bestOfN in /home/tjmisko/Projects/functionary-site/src/lib/flows.ts). It imports no component the home page lacks (Canvas, FlowSource, RunTable, Button are shared), so component internals are out of scope here.

Overall: the page is the stalest kind of content on the site. It is a seven-step walkthrough built around three embedded mock canvases, a verbatim flow-source snippet and a mock run table, all of which depict detail that is wrong today or re-ruled (v3 rulings, F110/F114, canvas redesign). It also frames the product as canvas-first for a reader who "never needs to open the source", which contradicts both the terminal/auto-mode direction since 2026-11-15 and the requested technical-tool framing. It links to /self-hosting as "Deployment" although nothing is distributable.

Drop: all three Canvas embeds and their captions, the reviewSource snippet (Field, Source::new, Judge::new, Check::new, .context, row: Row, lowercase settings, .record/.bool match no accepted flow on bleeding or integrate/f110), the mock run table (invented path format, receipt hashes, wrong Check-failure semantics), the Procedures section (four of five named procedures do not exist; Recover is removed; Consolidate/Match are being redesigned and hidden), "By default it cannot Run one" (reversed by auto mode), and "You never need to open the source".

Keep, as prose at structural level (these are the durable material for the reproducibility-for-trust argument): run pins (flow revision, block versions, table revisions); every effect recorded with a receipt and replayed rather than re-asked after a crash; Test as a dry run of the same pinned artifact with writes withheld, escalated to a Run that reuses the Test's receipts; failures kept as rows with a cause and not-run reported as such; Review parks a run durably and approval is bound to the specific output and its provenance; only a person answers a review; knowledge commit is an immutable revision marked partial on failed cells; the checker refuses loops, side I/O and literals and names the construct; fixes live in the flow.

Revise: "step"/"card" vocabulary (now block call / node), "resumes" (recovery is person-initiated), "the save is refused" (incomplete drafts are savable), one-to-one canvas/file claim (canvas is derived from source; not one node per binding), "Run it again next week" (currently sells repetition only; this is where the reproducibility-is-for-trust point belongs), and the Check-failure wording (a quote miss is result false on a kept row; Verified discharge is decided statically by the checker).

Things I checked myself: hand edits of tables exist as revisions in crates/functionary-flow-exec/src/commit.rs:110,261-273,912 and knowledge_edit (lib.rs:62), but as knowledge-table hand-edit revisions, not verified as in-place editing of run tables in the UI; CheckQuote semantics at crates/functionary-flow-blocks/src/check.rs:234-240; /self-hosting page exists at src/pages/self-hosting.astro. Not verified: whether a block can be renamed from the canvas (no rename op found in functionary-flow-edit/src/lib.rs by name search).
